requested.title: Issue-anchored runs can execute attacker-controlled ticket context on a local machine

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: The issue-launch route requires an authenticated user who can read the issue, but it accepts `localExec: true` and calls `launchAgentRun` with `triggeredBy: "button"` and the issue ID. `localExecRequested` and the independently repeated `createRun`, desktop-turn, and lease checks all delegate to `localRunScope`, which only excludes pull-request anchors, routines, chains, and non-button/chat triggers; an issue anchor is explicitly permitted. The local-turn route then prepares the job and issues a local execution lease for the run created by the launching user, so no cross-user run-claim bypass is needed for the victim's own desktop to execute it. `loadIssueContext` reads the issue title, description, and plan, as well as attachment metadata, and `buildAgentContextMessage` injects them into the initial model context; the builder itself states that an issue may originate from an anonymously submitted public-feedback post. Promotion preserves the feedback post title and body into a newly created issue's title and description, providing a concrete anonymous-content-to-issue path; a project collaborator can likewise supply or alter issue content. The prompt's delimiters and statement that ticket text is data are instructional text rather than an enforced provenance boundary, while local `bash` permissions allow commands unless they match the limited command guard's prohibited Git/destructive patterns. The local prompt also acknowledges that the whole disk is reachable, so a successful prompt injection can cause commands to run on the launcher's workstation without a per-command user approval. Git history shows the current local-scope mechanism was added as a third-party-content safeguard, but its data model omits issue provenance and no subsequent change adds that missing exclusion.
